title: Sum of Two Integers
directAnswer: Add two integers without using + or -. The insight: XOR is addition with the carries ignored (`a ^ b`), and `(a & b) << 1` is exactly those carries shifted into the next column. Loop — add the sum-without-carry, recompute the carry, repeat — until the carry is 0. In Python you must mask with `& 0xFFFFFFFF` to emulate fixed-width 32-bit overflow.

remember.formula:
while b != 0:
    carry = (a & b) << 1   # bits that carry into the next column
    a = a ^ b              # add without carrying
    b = carry              # now add the carry in
return a
rules: `a ^ b` is **sum without carry** — it's correct in every column where at most one bit is set.
`(a & b) << 1` is the **carry**: a column carries only when both bits are 1, and a carry lands one column to the **left**.
Loop until the carry (`b`) is 0 — each pass pushes carries leftward, and they must eventually run off the top.
In Java, `int` wraps at 32 bits for free. In **Python**, mask every step with **`& 0xFFFFFFFF`** and convert the high-bit-set result back to a negative via `~(a ^ 0xFFFFFFFF)`.
Subtraction reuses the same machine: `a - b = a + (~b + 1)` (two's complement negation).
whenToUse: Add/subtract integers without the + or − operators
Implement arithmetic from logic gates / simulate a full adder
Any 'do arithmetic with only bitwise ops' framing
antiSignals: You're allowed to use + → just use it; this trick is only for the artificial constraint
Floating-point or arbitrary-precision addition → the 32-bit bit model doesn't apply
Multiplication/division without operators → different shift-and-add structure
You need overflow to throw rather than wrap → this silently wraps like hardware
remember.takeaway: Sum of Two Integers teaches that addition IS two bit operations: XOR for the digit, AND-shifted for the carry — repeated until no carry remains, exactly like a row of full adders. The real interview test is Python's unbounded ints: without `& 0xFFFFFFFF` masking and sign conversion, negative results never terminate or come out wrong.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you understand addition at the bit level — that XOR is the carry-less sum and AND-then-shift is the carry — and whether you can emulate fixed-width two's-complement arithmetic in a language (Python) that has none.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Not masking in Python, so a negative input makes the carry loop run forever (the carry never clears in an infinite-precision int), or returning a huge positive number instead of converting the 32-bit pattern back to a signed negative.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain the full-adder analogy (XOR = sum bit, carry = AND), state why the loop terminates (carries march left and fall off), and proactively handle Python's masking and negative-result conversion without being prompted.

problemStatement: Given two integers `a` and `b`, return the sum of the two integers **without using the operators `+` and `-`**.
constraints: Result fits in a signed 32-bit integer
Bitwise operators (^, &, |, ~, <<, >>) and loops are allowed
understanding: Reimplement integer addition using only bitwise operations. Grade-school addition adds column by column and carries the overflow left; the bit version does the same with XOR producing each column's digit and AND-shift producing the carry. The subtlety is fixed-width signed arithmetic, which Python doesn't have natively.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the inputs be negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes (−1000 to 1000). Negatives use two's-complement bit patterns, which is why Python needs masking — its ints are infinite-precision and won't wrap like a 32-bit register.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which operators may I use?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Anything except + and −: XOR, AND, OR, NOT, and shifts are all fair game, plus loops and conditionals.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the result guaranteed to fit in 32 bits?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. That lets me mask to 32 bits in Python and rely on Java's natural int wraparound without worrying about a wider result.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should overflow throw or wrap?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It wraps, like real hardware. The 32-bit two's-complement model handles both positive and negative results consistently.

examples.explanation: 1 ^ 2 = 3 (no overlapping bits, so no carry). Carry (1 & 2) << 1 = 0 → done in one pass.
2 ^ 3 = 1 (sum without carry), carry (2 & 3) << 1 = 4. Next pass: 1 ^ 4 = 5, carry 0 → 5.
Two's-complement addition: the carries propagate through the sign bits and wrap, yielding 1. This is the case Python masking must get right.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Both simulate a full adder; the XOR/carry loop is the compact idiomatic form.

approaches.name: Full-Adder — Sum and Carry Per Bit
approaches.whenToMention: A clear first answer that mirrors hardware: 'I'll simulate a full adder across all 32 bit positions, tracking the sum bit and the carry.'
hints: Think about how a single column of binary addition works: two input bits plus an incoming carry produce a sum bit and an outgoing carry.
The sum bit is bitA ^ bitB ^ carry. The outgoing carry is set when at least two of the three inputs are 1.
Walk all 32 positions low to high, building the result bit by bit and threading the carry from one column to the next.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Exactly 32 iterations of constant-time bit logic, independent of the inputs → O(1) time and O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Simulate grade-school binary addition one column at a time. At bit position `i`, take `bitA`, `bitB`, and the incoming `carry`; the result bit is their three-way XOR, and the outgoing carry is `1` when two or more of them are set. Thread the carry into the next position and assemble the result.

**Why the sum bit is `bitA ^ bitB ^ carry`.** A binary column outputs `1` when an *odd* number of its three inputs are `1` — that's the definition of XOR over three bits. Two 1s sum to `10` (digit 0, carry out), three 1s sum to `11` (digit 1, carry out). XOR captures exactly the digit.

**Why the carry is the majority.** A column carries into the next when at least two inputs are `1`: `(bitA & bitB) | (carry & (bitA ^ bitB))`. The first term catches 'both inputs set'; the second catches 'exactly one input set plus an incoming carry'. Together that's the majority function — the classic full-adder carry.

**Why this handles negatives for free in Java.** Reading `(a >> i) & 1` across all 32 positions, including the sign bit at position 31, reconstructs the two's-complement value, and writing the sign bit back makes the result negative when appropriate. Java's `int` is already 32-bit two's complement, so no masking is needed. **In Python**, the bits are the same but the assembled `result` is a plain non-negative int, so if bit 31 is set we convert it back to a signed value with `~(result ^ 0xFFFFFFFF)`.
approaches.insight: This is literally a row of 32 full adders drawn in software — the same circuit inside every CPU's ALU. Seeing addition decompose into 'XOR for the digit, majority for the carry' demystifies why the compact XOR/carry loop (the next approach) works: it's this same logic, vectorised across all bits at once.

dryRun.intro: Walk positions 0..2; thread the carry. (Higher bits are 0.)

code.python:
def getSum(self, a: int, b: int) -> int:
    result = 0
    carry = 0
    for i in range(32):
        bit_a = (a >> i) & 1
        bit_b = (b >> i) & 1
        s = bit_a ^ bit_b ^ carry
        carry = (bit_a & bit_b) | (carry & (bit_a ^ bit_b))
        result |= (s << i)
    if result > 0x7FFFFFFF:
        result = ~(result ^ 0xFFFFFFFF)
    return result

java.explanation: Three-way XOR = 1 when an odd number of the three bits are set — the column's digit.
Majority function: carry out when at least two of the three inputs are 1.
Place the computed digit at position i. Position 31 sets the sign bit, making result negative when needed.

python.explanation: The sum bit for this column.
Carry out — same majority logic as the Java version.
Bit 31 set means the 32-bit pattern is negative; Python's int is non-negative, so convert it.
Reinterpret the 32-bit pattern as a signed two's-complement negative.

diagrams.title: Carry threading through the columns
diagrams.caption: Each column emits a sum bit and feeds a carry into the next column to the left.

edgeCases.behavior: Every column produces sum 0, carry 0 → result 0.
Carries propagate through the sign bit; in Python bit 31 is set so the conversion yields 1.

pitfalls: In Python, forgetting the final sign conversion — a negative answer comes back as a large positive (e.g. 4294967295 instead of −1).
Getting the carry logic wrong — it's the majority of three bits, not just bitA & bitB.
Looping fewer than 32 times and dropping the sign bit at position 31.

approaches.name: XOR Sum + Carry Loop (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The idiomatic answer. 'a ^ b adds without carrying; (a & b) << 1 is the carry; loop until the carry is zero.'
hints: Add 5 + 3 in your head ignoring carries column by column, then add the carries separately. Which bit op gives the carry-less sum, and which gives the carries?
a ^ b is the sum with every carry dropped. The positions that should have carried are exactly where both bits were 1: (a & b), shifted left by one.
Set a = a ^ b and b = (a & b) << 1, then repeat: keep folding the carry back in until there's no carry left (b == 0).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each pass moves the carries at least one bit position left; within a fixed 32-bit width they clear after at most ~32 passes → O(1) time and O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Split addition into two halves and iterate. `a ^ b` is the sum if you forget to carry; `(a & b) << 1` is precisely the carries you forgot, relocated to the column they belong in. Add those carries to the partial sum and repeat until there are no carries left.

**Why `a ^ b` is the carry-less sum.** Column by column, `0 + 0 = 0`, `0 + 1 = 1`, `1 + 0 = 1`, and `1 + 1 = 0` *with a carry*. Ignoring the carry, that truth table is exactly XOR. So `a ^ b` is correct in every column where the two bits don't both equal `1`.

**Why `(a & b) << 1` is the carry.** A column generates a carry only when *both* bits are `1` — that's `a & b`. And a carry always lands in the *next* column to the left, which is a left shift by one. So `(a & b) << 1` is the complete set of carries, already positioned. Adding it back to `a ^ b` corrects every column XOR got wrong.

**Why the loop terminates.** Each iteration's carry sits strictly to the left of the bits that produced it, so the carries march toward the high end and eventually fall off the top of the fixed width — at which point `b` (the carry) is `0` and `a` holds the answer. For 32-bit values this is at most ~32 passes.

**Why Python needs masking.** Python ints are arbitrary precision, so `(a & b) << 1` keeps growing and a negative input's carry *never* clears — the loop spins forever. Masking each step with `& 0xFFFFFFFF` confines the values to 32 bits so carries fall off as they would in a register. At the end, if bit 31 is set the pattern represents a negative number, which we recover with `~(a ^ 0xFFFFFFFF)`. Java needs none of this: its `int` already overflows at 32 bits.
approaches.insight: This is the full-adder from the previous approach collapsed into two parallel bitwise ops: XOR computes all 32 sum bits simultaneously, and AND-shift computes all 32 carries simultaneously. Re-feeding the carry is just 'add again with the leftovers' — the same way you'd hand-add `99 + 1` in two passes (sum digits, then propagate the carry).

dryRun.intro: Each pass: sum = a ^ b, carry = (a & b) << 1, then feed the carry back in.

java.explanation: Keep folding in the carry until none remains. int wraps at 32 bits, so carries fall off naturally.
Carry = columns where both bits are 1, shifted into the next column.
Sum without carry — correct wherever the bits didn't both equal 1.
Now 'add' the carry on the next pass.

python.explanation: 32-bit mask to emulate fixed-width overflow that Python's unbounded ints lack.
Only the low 32 bits count as the carry; without the mask a negative input loops forever.
Same carry computation; values may exceed 32 bits but the mask clamps them logically.
Bit 31 set → reinterpret the pattern as a signed two's-complement negative.

edgeCases.behavior: b is already 0, loop never runs → returns 0.
Carries propagate left through all 32 bits and fall off; masking lets b & mask reach 0 → returns 0. Without masking Python spins forever.

pitfalls: Omitting the mask in Python — negative inputs make (a & b) << 1 grow without bound and the loop never terminates.
Returning a & mask directly in Python without the sign conversion — negative answers come back as large positives.
Using `>>` instead of `<<` for the carry — the carry must move LEFT into the next-higher column.

commonMistakes: In Python, not masking with & 0xFFFFFFFF — negative inputs cause an infinite loop.
Returning the raw 32-bit pattern in Python without converting a set sign bit back to a negative number.
Mixing up the carry direction — it shifts LEFT, into the next-higher bit.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: No masking in Python (infinite loop)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Python ints are arbitrary-precision, so a negative input's carry keeps growing instead of overflowing away — the loop's exit condition b == 0 is never met.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
while b != 0:                 # never terminates for negative inputs
    carry = (a & b) << 1
    a = a ^ b
    b = carry
return a
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
mask = 0xFFFFFFFF
while (b & mask) != 0:        # only the low 32 bits gate the loop
    carry = (a & b) << 1
    a = a ^ b
    b = carry
a &= mask
return a if a <= 0x7FFFFFFF else ~(a ^ mask)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning the unsigned pattern instead of a signed value
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After masking, a result with bit 31 set is the two's-complement encoding of a negative number. Returning a & mask as-is yields a large positive (e.g. 4294967295) instead of −1.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
a &= 0xFFFFFFFF
return a                      # -1 comes back as 4294967295
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
a &= 0xFFFFFFFF
return a if a <= 0x7FFFFFFF else ~(a ^ 0xFFFFFFFF)   # convert to signed

patternNote: Bitwise full-adder. Recognise it whenever you must do arithmetic without the arithmetic operators. XOR is the carry-less sum, (a & b) << 1 is the carry, and you loop until the carry clears — the deeper lesson being fixed-width two's-complement emulation, which Python forces you to spell out with & 0xFFFFFFFF.
